Production readiness report · computer vision · October 2026

Marble race tracking: every simulated production gate passes

The complete system (colour detection, multi-camera fusion, occlusion handling, finish timing, live leaderboard) was run against 220 randomized and adversarial races, rendered by a 3D camera simulator with fourteen cameras mounted at about 45°, track walls, tunnels, perspective and marbles hiding each other. All simulated acceptance gates pass. The software is ready for hardware integration and on-site acceptance.

How it works

Every marble has a unique colour. Each camera finds marble-coloured pixels against the empty-track background, groups them by colour and maps each blob onto a calibrated centerline. From then on a marble is a single number: progress along the track in metres.

Because everything is in track metres, one or fourteen cameras is only configuration: a hand-off between cameras needs no special logic, tunnels and camera gaps are intervals on the track, and the leaderboard is a sort.

  • Identity: per-camera colour models in CIELAB, illumination-compensated every frame; a detection goes to a marble only if its colour is within reach of its best match.
  • Geometry: the centerline is calibrated at marble-centre height, and each blob is decomposed along and across the track using the camera's own perspective skew.
  • Tracking: one Kalman filter per marble on progress and speed, fed by every camera, with out-of-order frames and sudden reversals handled.
  • Ranking: an overtake is shown only when it is seen, larger than half a marble plus 2σ, and (near that threshold) held for 100 ms. Nobody passes a marble whose position is uncertain.
  • Finish: a least-squares fit of the frames around the line gives each time and an honest uncertainty; close calls are flagged.

Fourteen cameras at 45°

The 14 segment cameras are simulated as real pinhole cameras roughly 0.4–0.9 m from the track and about 45° above it, looking from behind, ahead, both sides and the diagonals. A depth buffer handles every occlusion.

  • Perspective scale. The same marble spans 7–29 px depending on where it is in the view. Expected blob size is tabulated along each camera's section at calibration.
  • Height parallax. A marble's centre is 12.5 mm above the track. The centerline is recorded at marble-centre height (roll a marble along it), so parallax cancels.
  • Skew. Seen at an angle, the cross-track direction is not perpendicular to the track's image. Plain nearest-pixel projection errs by up to 10 mm for marbles in the outer lanes; the oblique projection brings that to a median of 0.5 mm (p95 1.4 mm) over 420 placements.
  • Walls and line-of-sight occlusion. Track walls hide the lower part of marbles in the near lane, and marbles lined up along the line of sight hide each other. Partly hidden blobs carry a larger, correlated uncertainty; fully hidden marbles cannot gain places and cannot be passed on prediction.
  • Section edges. In an angled view a marble just past the end of a camera's section can poke into it. Only blobs at least 85 % inside the section are accepted, so nothing is reported from a clipped fragment.
  • Lighting. Under a 20 % dimming, the light-grey walls in these views drifted from the stored background and produced phantom detections. Per-frame illumination gain on background and colours removed them.

Stress suite: 150 randomized races

Ten random races per scenario and rig. Each race has ten marbles, overtakes throughout, unsynchronised cameras, sensor noise and per-camera colour casts. The board is scored against ground truth 30 times per second.

Hidden marbles are the only real source of disagreement. Inside a tunnel nobody can see who leads; the board shows those marbles as hidden and holds them until they reappear. Among visible marbles the strict score counts a correct overtake as wrong for the few frames before it is confirmed; within the 100 ms display budget used for broadcast graphics every race scores at least 100.00 %.

What is guaranteed, and how we know

These properties hold by construction. Property-based fuzzing checks them after every frame of hundreds of random input streams with clutter, ambiguous colours, duplicate and out-of-order frames, NaNs and silent cameras.

InvariantMechanism and check
One identity per detection, one detection per marble per frameHungarian assignment with colour ratio test; fuzz-tested every frame
No marble gains a place while it is hiddenRank rule; fuzz-tested every frame
Nobody passes a marble whose position is uncertainPass threshold includes the hidden marble's growing variance; chain rule keeps visible passes
No rank flicker below half a marble's widthMargin + 2σ, and 100 ms confirmation near the threshold
Finish order is correct or explicitly flaggedFlag below 3σ of the two fitted times; provisional times claim no better than half a frame
Corrupt input never reaches the filterNaN/inf, wrong palette size, empty candidates dropped; fuzz-tested
Filter covariance stays symmetric positive semi-definiteChecked after every update in fuzzing
Bounded latencyFixed 50 ms reorder window; edge nodes drop late frames instead of queueing

Real time, on ordinary hardware

Live run: the full system in wall-clock time

Edge-node processes grab frames from the virtual cameras on the clock, detect, and stream detections to the fusion process, which publishes the leaderboard ten times a second.

52 / 62 mscapture → fused, p50 / p9515 angled cameras, 4 edge processes; includes the 50 ms reorder window
100.0%live board correct6,451 frames, 1121 dropped as late
57 msoverhead-camera rig, p952,797 frames, 290 dropped

Measured on a 4-core cloud container that also renders all 15 virtual 3D camera images in Python. That rendering, not detection, saturates the container, so edge nodes drop late frames (1,121 here) to keep latency bounded. Real cameras deliver frames without that cost.

Ready for what, exactly

Verified in simulation

  • Identity, association, fusion, occlusion logic, ranking rules and finish timing, end to end against exact ground truth.
  • Angled-camera geometry: perspective, skew, parallax, walls and line-of-sight occlusion.
  • Failure handling: dead cameras, frame loss, network jitter, lighting drift.
  • Real-time operation with separate edge and fusion processes.

Needs on-site acceptance

  • Real marbles and optics. Glass swirls, transparency and reflections of neighbours are not simulated. Calibration measures every colour pair's separation before race day.
  • Real lighting. Slow drift is handled; flicker is not. Flicker-free DC LED lighting is a requirement.
  • Collisions. Simulated marbles never knock each other off the track. A marble that leaves is reported lost and re-acquired by colour.
  • Absolute timing offset. One-sided lighting shifts every marble's visible centre equally (about 0.2 ms at the line). It does not change the order; a single light-gate run calibrates it out.

Path to go-live, about 11–12 weeks

  1. Hardware bring-up (2 weeks). Two segment cameras, finish camera, lighting, camera SDK adapter, PTP.
  2. Field trial on one segment (2 weeks). Real marbles at 45°: identity ≥ 99.5 % on 20 annotated runs; every colour pair separable.
  3. Full rig (3 weeks). All cameras calibrated; live overlay with p95 latency ≤ 150 ms; camera-failure drill.
  4. Acceptance (2 weeks). 50 recorded races against hand-annotated truth, the same gates as above.
  5. Hardening (2–3 weeks). C++ hot loop, monitoring, frame archive for audit, 4-hour soak test.
